chunks.title: AI-native, human in charge
chunks.text: How Habib builds with AI. I plan with agents, code with AI pair programmers and keep every decision reviewable. My own LangGraph workflow turns an idea into approved specs, with me as the human in the loop. Step 1, Plan: LangGraph agents clarify, scope and write specs. Step 2, Human review: I approve or reject every step (HITL). Step 3, Build: Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, reviewed by me. Step 4, Test: TDD, k6 load and stress tests. Step 5, Ship: CI/CD tests and builds every push. AI toolkit I use every week: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, LangGraph, Human-in-the-loop, RAG pipelines, Vector embeddings, Cosine similarity, Prompt engineering, GPT-OSS via Groq. AI drafts, I decide. Every AI-written change goes through my review, tests and CI before it ships. Questions? The guide in the corner knows the whole site.

Status: Bachelor project · in progress · due Jan 2027. Engagement threshold: 0.1 (Design parameter from the PRD). First, opt-in capture: Local. Technologies: RAG pipeline, Embeddings, TDD.

chunks.title: TopicTrail: Solution
chunks.text: TopicTrail. A memory for what you browse: it keeps the pages you actually engaged with and finds them again by meaning, not only by keyword. The planned pipeline. Planned: capture is local-first and opt-in. Only pages you engaged with past an engagement threshold are kept (0.1 in the current design). Planned: retrieval is a RAG pipeline that combines keyword search with semantic search over vector embeddings, so a half-remembered idea still finds the page.

chunks.title: Ridly, carpooling for Android and iOS
chunks.text: Ridly, carpooling for Android and iOS (featured project). Drivers post trips, passengers book seats, and both chat in real time. Planned with my LangGraph workflow, load-tested with k6. Habib's role: Built solo. Trip search p95: 96 ms (At 300 virtual users, in a k6 ramp to 1,500). Commits, built solo: 387. Technologies: Kotlin MP, SwiftUI, NestJS, LangGraph, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot. Code: https://github.com/Habibwasi/HOP-KMP.

chunks.title: Ridly: Problem
chunks.text: Ridly. A carpooling app for Denmark: drivers post trips, passengers book seats, and both chat in real time, on Android and iOS from one Kotlin codebase. Why it needed to exist. Plenty of cars in Denmark drive the same commute every weekday, or a long trip between cities, with empty seats. The people who could fill them usually find out through group chats and posts: no search by route and date, no agreed price, and no record of who has paid. Ridly puts both sides in one app. A passenger searches a route and a date, books a seat at a price worked out from the distance, and knows the trip is on. A driver fills seats on a drive they were making anyway and splits its cost.

chunks.title: Ridly: My role
chunks.text: Ridly. What I built. I built Ridly alone: the shared Kotlin Multiplatform module, the Android app, the iOS app and the NestJS API. All 387 commits in the repository are mine. Money stays between the two riders. After the ride the passenger pays the driver in MobilePay, and the app records “paid”, “received” or a dispute. Leaving out a payment provider kept the first version free of fees and contracts; the cost is that payment rests on trust, which ratings and the dispute flow back up. Prices follow SKAT’s rate of 2.28 kr per kilometre, split across the seats, so a seat costs a share of the drive, not a fare. Every amount is stored as whole øre and only turned into kroner on screen, so no rounding creeps in. Two kinds of trip, because commutes and long journeys behave differently. A daily commute keeps 30 days of trips ahead of itself. A one-off long trip only runs if enough passengers book before a deadline: a background job checks at the deadline, and if the minimum isn’t met it cancels the bookings and tells everyone.

chunks.title: Ridly: AI in the build
chunks.text: Ridly. AI in the build. Planning ran through my LangGraph workflow (AI_Workflow_Global). Agents draft each spec, and a human-in-the-loop gate stops at every step until I approve it or send it back. Claude Code and GitHub Copilot wrote code against rules kept in the repository. Agent.md records the architecture decisions and the verified library versions, and tells the agent to stop and ask when a request conflicts with them instead of inventing a change. A bug-audit skill gives Copilot a checklist of Ridly's own failure modes, such as missing Koin registrations, ViewModel idempotency guards and how money is displayed. One correction shows why those rules exist. To run database migrations on Railway, the agent added the connection URLs to the Prisma schema, the way Prisma 6 did it. Ridly runs Prisma 7, which moved that setting out of the schema, so the change broke the deploy. I reverted it within minutes and kept the connection in prisma.config.ts, and the verified-versions list in Agent.md now tells the agent which version it is writing for.

chunks.title: Ridly: Solution
chunks.text: Ridly. A carpooling app for Denmark: drivers post trips, passengers book seats, and both chat in real time, on Android and iOS from one Kotlin codebase. From empty seat to settled trip. Drivers post a trip and review its price. Passengers search by route and date, book a seat, and chat with the driver in real time before the ride. Saved search alerts tell passengers when a matching trip appears. After the ride, the passenger pays the driver directly with MobilePay, and the app tracks each settlement until it is marked as paid. Driver and passenger rate each other, and drivers get a dashboard and a downloadable report of what they earned, for their taxes.

chunks.title: Ridly: Architecture
chunks.text: Ridly. How it fits together. One Kotlin Multiplatform module holds the domain models, the repositories, Ktor networking and the ViewModels, wired with Koin. Android renders them in Compose Multiplatform, and the iOS app wraps the same ViewModels for SwiftUI, so the business logic is written once. The ViewModels follow MVI: the screen sends events, renders an immutable state, and handles one-shot effects such as navigation. The backend is a NestJS 11 API on PostgreSQL through Prisma. Supabase handles sign-in, and the API checks the token on every request. Socket.IO carries the chat, Mapbox turns addresses into routes and distances for pricing, and push notifications go out through Firebase Cloud Messaging and Apple’s push service. BullMQ on Redis runs the background jobs: deadline checks for one-off trips, extending recurring trips and matching search alerts. Trip origins and destinations are PostGIS geography points with spatial indexes, which is what trip search runs on. Sentry reports errors from all three apps.

chunks.title: Ridly: Test evidence
chunks.text: Ridly. Proof it holds up. A k6 load test ramped from 300 to 600 to 1,500 virtual users against the API. At the 300-user stage, trip search had a p95 of 96 ms. A second k6 script attacks the API on purpose: missing fields, huge strings, broken tokens, unknown IDs and a burst of 50 requests a second on search. It fails if a single request gets a server error. CI runs the shared module's unit tests and builds the Android app on every push to main and every pull request into it. It builds the iOS app too, but that step can't fail the run yet, so an iOS build error would slip through. A review of the whole codebase lists what isn't solved yet, and that is the next work: two people booking the last seat at the same moment can both get it, completing a trip can fail halfway through creating the payment records, and creating the same recurring trip twice isn't fully prevented. The backend's own tests don't run in CI yet either.

chunks.title: Validation Portal, research for founders
chunks.text: Validation Portal, research for founders (featured project). Surveys, customer interviews and an LLM verdict with themes, key quotes and next steps, so founders test ideas before building. Habib's role: Built solo. Commits: 111. Demo online: Live. Technologies: TypeScript, React, Supabase, GPT-OSS 20B via Groq. Code: https://github.com/Habibwasi/Validation-Portal. Live demo: https://validation-portal.vercel.app.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Problem
chunks.text: Validation Portal. A research tool for founders: surveys, customer interviews and an LLM verdict, so they test an idea before they build it. Why it needed to exist. It started with an idea of my own. Before building it, I wanted to know whether anyone actually had the problem, and the evidence ended up scattered: survey answers in one tool, interview notes in another, and no honest way to tell whether the signal was strong enough. Early founders hit the same wall. They build first and ask later, or they ask leading questions and hear what they hoped to hear. Validation Portal keeps the hypotheses, the survey and the conversations in one place, and asks what the evidence actually says.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: My role
chunks.text: Validation Portal. What I built. I built it alone, from the database schema to the serverless functions. All 111 commits in the repository are mine. AI drafts, the founder decides. Generated survey questions arrive as unsaved drafts and only reach the live survey once the founder saves them, and every question is scored against The Mom Test, with a rewrite suggested for any that lead the respondent. The AI never runs in the browser. On the first day I moved the model call into a serverless function that checks the Supabase session first, so the API key stays on the server and anonymous traffic can’t spend the quota. Anyone can try it without an account. Guests sign in anonymously through Supabase behind a Cloudflare Turnstile check, and an hourly job deletes their data once it is seven days old. A guest who adds an email keeps everything, because the user ID doesn’t change.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: AI in the build
chunks.text: Validation Portal. AI in the build. I built it with GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, reviewing what they wrote before it went in. I also used the project to try out models for the product’s own AI. It started on OpenAI, moved to Google Gemini, then to Groq, where it now runs GPT-OSS 20B. Because every call goes through the serverless functions, each switch stayed on the server side.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Solution
chunks.text: Validation Portal. A research tool for founders: surveys, customer interviews and an LLM verdict, so they test an idea before they build it. From hunch to verdict. Founders write their assumptions as hypotheses ("I believe [customer] has [problem] and will pay [price] for [solution]"), share a public survey, and log customer interviews with pain scores, quotes and tags. An LLM reads the aggregated numbers and up to 15 quotes, then returns a verdict with themes, key quotes, next steps and a call on each hypothesis. The verdict follows fixed rules: a strong signal needs at least five interviews, 70% pain and 60% concept interest. Founders can share the result as a read-only report link. In the Survey Builder, AI drafts questions from the idea’s description and checks each one for bias. One click translates the survey into eight languages (Arabic, Bengali, Danish, French, German, Hindi, Spanish and Turkish), so respondents answer one question at a time in their own language, without logging in.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Architecture
chunks.text: Validation Portal. How it fits together. A React 19 single-page app (Vite, TypeScript) talks to Supabase: PostgreSQL with row-level security on every table, so each user, guest or not, only reads their own data. The AI calls run in Vercel serverless functions: one for the verdict, the question drafts and the bias check, and one for translation. They check the Supabase session before calling GPT-OSS 20B (openai/gpt-oss-20b) on Groq. Resend emails the owner on each survey response, and Cloudflare Turnstile guards every sign-in, sign-up and guest session.

chunks.title: Validation Portal: Test evidence
chunks.text: Validation Portal. Proof it works. Validation Portal has no automated tests or CI yet. The evidence is the live demo, which anyone can use as a guest, plus the demo video and the diagrams above.

chunks.title: How this guide works
chunks.text: The assistant in the corner is a small retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over this site. It answers only from the site's own text, cites where each answer comes from, and says "I don't know" when nothing fits. Build step, Chunk: At build time, every case study section, project, the intro, availability, QA record and this page become one chunk each. Missing content is skipped, never indexed. Build step, Embed: Each chunk is embedded with gte-small, a 384-dimension open model that runs locally through Transformers.js. No embedding API. Build step, Ship: Chunks and vectors are written to a JSON file in the repository, so the index always deploys with the content it was built from. Request step, Limit: Each visitor gets 10 questions per 10 minutes, and the whole site 90 a day, to stay inside the Groq free tier. When a limit is reached, or Groq is unavailable, the guide says it is busy and lists the parts of the site that match the question instead, found by search alone. Request step, Embed: The question is embedded with the same model, inside the serverless function. Request step, Retrieve: Keyword search (BM25) and vector search (cosine) each rank the chunks; reciprocal rank fusion merges them, and the top 4 become the sources. Request step, Generate: GPT-OSS 120B on Groq answers in a few sentences, only from the numbered sources, and cites them. Request step, Cite: Source links come from the chunks themselves, never from the model's text. If no chunk shares a keyword with the question and none is close in meaning, the model isn't called at all; the guide says "I don't know". When sources are found but don't answer the question, the model is told to say "I don't know" too. GPT-OSS 120B (openai/gpt-oss-120b) on Groq, with low reasoning effort and a short answer limit. The model ID is one value in the code, so swapping it is a one-line change. About 20 recruiter questions run against the real route every night: the expected source must be retrieved, the answer must cite a source and contain the key facts, and out-of-scope questions must get "I don't know". A few answers are checked for faithfulness by a second model call. A few dozen chunks fit easily in memory, so there is no vector database. With many more documents, the same index format would move to Postgres with pgvector.
